label: Curvature of Plane Curves
notes: This chapter opens Part Three on printed pages 97 to 105. We measure how sharply a plane curve bends by three equivalent stories: the force needed to steer a moving point, the radius of the best fitting circle, and the rate at which the tangent direction turns as we walk along the arc.

label: What Should Curvature Measure?
notes: Before any formula we agree on what we want. A straight line should have curvature zero, a tight circle more curvature than a wide one, and the number should not care how fast a particle traces the path. These three demands already force curvature to be one over a length, the geometry of the local bend.

label: Curvature as a Steering Force
notes: Needham's first picture is physical. A point of unit mass moving at unit speed feels a force perpendicular to its motion that bends the trajectory. The amount of inward force required to hold the point on the curve is exactly the curvature. Straight motion needs no force, so its curvature vanishes, matching intuition.

label: The Osculating Circle
notes: Take three nearby points on the curve and pass a circle through them. As the outer two slide into the middle one, this circle settles onto a single limiting circle that kisses the curve. Its radius R is the radius of curvature, and the curvature is its reciprocal. The circle sits on the concave side.

label: Curvature Equals One Over R
notes: For a circle of radius R the definition must give a constant, since the bend is the same everywhere. The osculating circle of any curve is the circle whose bending matches the curve at that instant, so the curve and circle share tangent and second order contact. Hence the fundamental formula kappa equals one over R.

label: Tangent Turning Along the Arc
notes: Walk along the curve and watch the tangent direction. Its angle phi changes as you advance. Curvature is the rate at which that angle turns per unit length travelled, the derivative of phi with respect to arc length s. A sharp bend turns the tangent quickly over a short arc, so kappa is large there.

label: Arc Length and the Unit Tangent
notes: Reparametrize by arc length so the point moves at unit speed. Then the tangent vector T has constant length one and can only rotate, never stretch. Its derivative with respect to s is perpendicular to T and points toward the centre of the osculating circle. The length of that derivative is the curvature.

label: Newton's Vanishing Triangle
notes: Newton derived curvature from a tiny triangle. Over an arc of length delta-s the tangent swings by a small angle delta-phi. The chord, the change in tangent, and the radius form similar triangles that collapse as the arc shrinks. In the limit the surviving ratio delta-phi over delta-s is precisely the curvature, one over R.

label: Reading the Limit Carefully
notes: The triangle argument only works because the discarded pieces vanish faster than the kept ones. The chord and the arc agree to first order, and the angle equals the arc over the radius for a circle. Tracking which quantities are first order and which are higher order is the heart of every infinitesimal curvature computation.

label: Signed Curvature and Orientation
notes: In the plane we can give curvature a sign by choosing a sense of turning. Counterclockwise bending is positive, clockwise negative, and an inflection where the curve switches sides has curvature zero. The unsigned magnitude is one over R, while the sign records which way the osculating circle lies relative to the oriented tangent.

label: Worked Example: The Tractrix
notes: The tractrix is the path of a weight dragged on a taut string of fixed length whose end moves along a line. Its defining property is that the tangent segment from the curve to the axis always has the same length. Computing its curvature turns the abstract definition into a concrete measurement we can check numerically.

label: Summary: Three Faces of Curvature
notes: We met one quantity wearing three masks: the steering force on a unit-speed point, the reciprocal radius of the osculating circle, and the turning rate of the tangent. They agree because each measures the same local bend. This single number kappa is the foundation for the curvature of surfaces studied next.
